question: Describe how you would build our new public website on AEM Sites with Edge Delivery Services, including the blocks and page templates our marketing team will author with.
kb:
Our approach
- Your site is built on Edge Delivery Services and accepted for migration and launch, with authoring set up and Brand Visibility's edge routing working on your outer CDN.

How we would do it
- Turn the Brand Visibility findings and your search strategy into the site plan and information architecture, and agree the page set, templates and integrations.
- Design and build the block library and page templates on Edge Delivery Services, with the code managed and deployed from a GitHub repository.
- Set up authoring where your authors will work, in AEM Authoring, with an instant URL to review and share changes.
- Set up the CDN route with your team, through your own Akamai CDN, and connect the agreed integrations.
- Build the agreed pages, testing each change for a Lighthouse score of 100 on mobile and desktop and against the agreed quality checks.
- Set up Brand Visibility's Optimize at Edge routing on your outer CDN with your CDN team, allow the AdobeEdgeOptimize/1.0 user agent in robots.txt and bot rules, and test the route.

What you get
- A working Edge Delivery site with the agreed pages
- Block library and page templates
- Configured authoring, CDN route and integrations
- Optimize at Edge routing, tested on the CDN
- Build record

Timeline and effort
- Planning estimate: 960 hours.
- This runs during the build, once discovery has agreed the scope.

Risk we manage
- Scope growing during the build: we agree the page set, templates and integrations before building, and test each change against the agreed checks as we go.

What we would need from you
- Decisions on the page set, templates and integrations before the build starts

question: Our current site runs on Drupal 9 and holds about 3,400 pages and 900 PDF documents, including state rate filings. Describe how you would migrate this content, what you would retire, and how you would preserve URLs.
kb:
Our approach
- You told us: Your current site runs on Drupal 9 and holds about 3,400 pages and 900 PDF documents, including state rate filings.
- Your agreed pages are on the new site with their titles, descriptions and structured data in place, and every retired URL redirects to its new page.

How we would do it
- Map your current site to the new one page by page, documents included, using your analytics and search data, and mark each page and document to keep, merge or retire.
- Run Adobe's importer on an example of each page type so your authors can agree the structure, then migrate the agreed pages into Edge Delivery documents and blocks.
- Build the redirect map, with every retired page and document URL in the redirects spreadsheet, and set up bulk metadata and sitemaps for the new site.
- Assess your current sites, vendors and content debt through stakeholder interviews and a review of your analytics, and write the current-state assessment.
- Inventory your components and templates, find the duplicates, and agree a rationalized list of what to keep, merge or retire.
- Set the target architecture, the integrations and the governance model in workshops with your executives and technical leads.

What you get
- Migrated pages in Edge Delivery documents and blocks
- Redirect map
- Metadata and sitemap records
- Current-state assessment
- Component rationalization list

Timeline and effort
- Planning estimate: 400 hours.
- This runs during the build, once discovery has agreed the scope.

Risk we manage
- Losing search value when URLs change: every retired URL gets a redirect, and crawl and link checks must pass before launch.

question: Describe how you would make the new site conform to WCAG 2.2 Level AA, and how accessibility would be checked before each release.
kb:
Our approach
- Your templates are tested against WCAG 2.2 Level AA before launch, and each release is checked the same way, with a record of the results.

How we would do it
- Agree WCAG 2.2 Level AA as the target with your team, then audit your current templates and a sample of pages and record each gap.
- Build each component and template to meet every Level A and AA success criterion, including visible focus, target size, color contrast, headings, form labels and text alternatives.
- Test every template with an automated scan, keyboard-only use and screen readers such as NVDA, JAWS and VoiceOver, and log each issue against its WCAG success criterion.
- Train your authors to write alternative text, headings, link text and table headers, with a checklist to run before they publish each page.
- Set a release gate: each release passes an automated scan and a manual keyboard and screen reader check of changed templates, with no new A or AA failures.

What you get
- Accessibility audit of templates and sample pages
- WCAG 2.2 AA test plan and release checklist
- Issue log mapped to WCAG success criteria
- Author guide and checklist for accessible content

Timeline and effort
- Planning estimate: about 60 to 240 hours for this work.
- This runs during the build, once discovery has agreed the scope.

Risk we manage
- New content that falls below AA after launch: we train your authors and give them a checklist to run before they publish each page.

What we would need from you
- An accessibility lead on your side who approves the test plan and signs off each release

question: Describe how you would achieve and keep strong Core Web Vitals and Lighthouse scores on the new site.
kb:
Our approach
- In Adobe's Keeping it 100 guidance, the delayed phase of page loading holds third-party tags and other assets that are not material to the experience.
- Your key templates launch at their agreed Lighthouse scores, every later release is tested against them, and real visitor data shows any page that slips.

How we would do it
- Measure your current site's Core Web Vitals and Lighthouse scores for each key template, on mobile and desktop, as the baseline we compare against after launch.
- Agree a Lighthouse score per key template for release tests, and Google's good thresholds for real visitors: LCP 2.5 seconds, INP 200 milliseconds and CLS 0.1, at the 75th percentile.
- Build each template so what the first screen needs loads first and third-party tags load last, and check that the CDN caches pages, code and images.
- Test every release against the agreed Lighthouse score before it goes live, and hold any change that drops a key template below its target until it is fixed.
- Track real visitors' Core Web Vitals after launch against the agreed thresholds and the baseline, find the pages and elements that slow them down, and fix the worst first.

What you get
- Baseline and target scores for each key template
- Third-party tag inventory with a load plan
- A performance test in every release
- Post-launch Core Web Vitals report

Timeline and effort
- Planning estimate: about 24 to 96 hours for this work.

Risk we manage
- Third-party tags added after launch slowing pages again: we agree with your tag owners that each new tag passes the same release test, and watch real visitor data.

question: Akamai is our enterprise CDN and must remain in front of the site. Describe how you would configure Akamai with Edge Delivery Services, including caching, purging and security headers.
kb:
Our approach
- You told us: Akamai is your enterprise CDN and must remain in front of the site.
- Your CDN stays in front of the site, with caching, purges, HTTPS and security rules tested on stage before your live traffic switches over.

How we would do it
- Map your CDN setup with your CDN team: who owns it, the change windows, our access, the paths each origin serves, and which changes we prepare and your team applies.
- Build a stage configuration on your CDN that points each path to its origin, such as the Edge Delivery origin, whose cache headers set the TTL, or the AEM-managed CDN.
- Set up purging: push invalidation in the production CDN configuration on Edge Delivery, or for the AEM-managed CDN its purge API token and a matching purge on yours.
- Review security with your security team: enforce HTTPS, set the X-AEM-Edge-Key where your CDN sits in front of the AEM-managed CDN, and keep the edge rules your policy requires.
- Run load, caching, purge, redirect and page speed tests on stage, then switch your CDN's origin, or DNS where the hostname changes, and hand your CDN team a runbook.

What you get
- Stage and production CDN configuration
- Load, caching, purge and page speed test results
- Security settings record signed off by your team
- Cutover plan and CDN runbook

Timeline and effort
- Planning estimate: about 24 to 96 hours for this work.

Risk we manage
- Changes held up by CDN access or change windows: we agree owners and windows in discovery and prepare each change for your CDN team to apply.

question: Every page that mentions rates, coverage or claims must be approved by our Compliance team before it is published. Describe the review and approval workflow you would set up for authors and reviewers.
kb:
Our approach
- You told us: Every page that mentions rates, coverage or claims must be approved by your Compliance team before it is published.
- Every page change is approved before it goes live, urgent corrections included, and each published version can be traced to its approval.

How we would do it
- Map your review route by site section with your content owners: who writes, who checks legal or safety wording, who approves, and who covers urgent corrections out of hours.
- Keep the workflows non-transient so their history is saved, create a page version at each publish, keep both for your retention period, and test every route with your reviewers.
- Create the site on AEM Author from the Edge Delivery Services with AEM authoring site template, and link your Edge Delivery code to it as the content source.
- Set up push invalidation for the Edge Delivery paths, and keep every other page on AEM Publish until its phase comes.
- Set the design-system and component standards every team follows, and write them up in a short standards guide for designers, developers and authors.
- Build two Skills, and validate them on agreed pilot pages and templates on your AEM route.

What you get
- Publish permissions for author and approver groups
- Publishing test results
- Phase plan with paths and rollback steps
- Roles and approvals model
- Approved brand context

Timeline and effort
- Planning estimate: 328 hours.
- This runs during the build, once discovery has agreed the scope.

Risk we manage
- A page going live unreviewed: we remove the authors' right to publish, so every change, urgent corrections included, passes an approver and leaves a record.

question: We will not license Adobe Target in this phase. Describe how you would run A/B tests on the new quote-start page without it.
kb:
Our approach
- You told us: You will not license Adobe Target in this phase.
- Each A/B test on your pages runs to an agreed plan, with each visitor's variant in your analytics, and you keep only the changes the results support.

How we would do it
- Agree a test plan with your team for each test: the hypothesis, one primary metric such as form starts, guardrail metrics, the sample size and the run time.
- Build the challenger as a copy of the control page that changes one thing, such as the headline or call to action, and keep it out of search indexes.
- Send the experiment ID and the variant each visitor sees into your analytics data with every page view and conversion, so each result can be split by variant.
- Check each variant before launch: preview both pages, confirm the tracking records the right variant, start with an even traffic split, and check the split again once real traffic arrives.
- Decide each test at its planned sample size from the primary metric's lift and confidence by variant, then publish the winner as the page and log the learning.

What you get
- Test plan with hypothesis, metrics and sample size
- Challenger pages, kept out of search indexes
- Experiment and variant tracking in your analytics
- Results readout and learnings log for each test

Timeline and effort
- Planning estimate: about 20 to 80 hours a month.
- This runs every month from the month after launch.

Risk we manage
- Calling a winner too early on too little traffic: we set the sample size and run time before launch, and decide only when the test reaches them.

question: Describe how you would use Adobe Brand Visibility to measure how AI assistants such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity describe Cedar Prairie and our products, and how you would report it to us.
kb:
Our approach
- You have an approved prompt portfolio mapped to your content, and a baseline plan for how your brand's presence in AI answers is measured.

How we would do it
- Run two discovery workshops with your marketing and product leads to agree customer intents, competitors and the business measures that matter.
- Map each intent to the content that should answer it, and note the gaps where no content exists today.
- Configure the monitoring portfolio in Brand Visibility from your approved prompt plan, with the agreed markets, languages and competitors, and confirm each pilot user can open the workspace.
- Build Workspace reports for the agreed conversation, recommendation and purchase measures, limited to what the selected data supports.
- Connect and curate the approved content sources for the agreed products, with your reviewers signing off each source.
- Map the agreed banking or insurance discovery questions that Brand Visibility tracks to approved Brand Concierge sources, with an owner for each source.

What you get
- Responsibilities for each measure
- Configured monitoring portfolio in Brand Visibility
- Measure definitions
- A live Brand Concierge experience on the agreed pages
- Question-to-source map

Timeline and effort
- Planning estimate: 168 hours.

Risk we manage
- Prompts that miss what your customers ask, since AI platforms do not disclose those questions: we build them from agreed intents and your evidence, and your reviewers approve them.
catalog:
Our approach
- Brand Visibility sends aggregate AI-agent activity (from CDN logs, by URL and host) into CJA through an Experience Platform source. AI-referred visits and conversions come from CJA's own web data, and Brand Visibility reads those results for its business impact view.
- Brand Visibility runs the prompts you choose on a recurring basis across the AI platforms it supports and records how your brand appears in each answer and how that changes over time. It measures the prompts you monitor: the questions people put to AI assistants themselves are not disclosed by the platforms.

- The dashboards report the percentage of prompts where your brand is mentioned, how often your website is used as a source, share of voice and sentiment, and compare you with the other brands you choose to track in each market.

What we would do
- For Cedar Prairie Mutual Insurance Company, we will configure the supported Brand Visibility bot-data connection and map URLs and hosts; we will identify AI-referred visits in the existing CJA web data with a derived field on AI referring domains; and we will align observed AI-referral and conversion measures with existing CJA data.

What we would need from you

question: What uptime commitments apply to the proposed Adobe products?
catalog:
Uptime and recovery
- Adobe posts the availability of all its services at status.adobe.com.¹
- Edge Delivery Services: has the same service level agreement as AEM as a Cloud Service and runs on multiple CDNs, so delivery can switch to another CDN during an outage. Adobe acknowledges every incident within 15 minutes.²,³,⁴
- AEM Sites: a 99.99% service level is a separately licensed option, applied together with an Additional Publish Region on the same program. Sandboxes are not covered by the service level.⁵ Content can be restored from continuous backups within the past 24 hours or from system backups within the past seven days; a restore covers content, not code. In a data-region outage, Adobe restores staging and production from off-site backups.⁶

- The uptime and recovery targets you need.
